style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: The bridging recommendation.
A lot of students add one at the end of the rebuttal paragraph. Let's see what it is, when it helps, and when it hurts.
A bridging recommendation says: okay, I choose my position. But I still see some logic in the other position, so I move a little toward it.
It's not the golden mean. The golden mean is right in the middle. This isn't in the middle. It's small.
It's eighty-twenty, not fifty-fifty. Eighty percent my side, and I move a little toward the other side.
For the essay, I'm offering a possible solution to the problem raised in the counter-argument. They say: there's a problem here. And I say: I have a solution to your problem.
And that makes my weakening of the counter-argument stronger.
For the rater, we show critical thinking, and that we really considered the other view.
It's like saying, I'm not deaf. I understand there are disadvantages on my side, and I want to help solve them.
And there's a weakening through the back door here too. I solved a problem that hurts them. If it's solved, there's less reason to choose their side. It's fine to stay with mine.
Where do we write it? At the end of the rebuttal paragraph, after our weakening.
So there was a counter-argument, I weakened it, and then I say: you know what, I'll also move a little toward it. It adds a bit more to the weakening.
The recommendation has to connect directly to the counter-argument. Not: they talked about one thing, and I recommend something else.
For and against school uniforms. One counter-argument: students want self-expression, to dress how they like. Another one is economic. Buying school shirts is an unnecessary cost for parents.

Say the rebuttal raises the economic argument, I weaken it, and then I suggest a free-dress Friday. Nice recommendation, but it's not connected. Parents still have to buy shirts for the rest of the week.
It would fit perfectly if the counter-argument were self-expression. Give them room to express themselves on Fridays, and uniforms the rest of the week, because of the other advantages I presented.
In the camera task, there's a real concern about privacy. So we can create control mechanisms.

For example, set up a specific body. The database and the information don't go to every police officer in every station. Just a special unit, a small number of people, under ongoing supervision. And only they can access the information.
And if some police unit wants the information, it has to apply to that body, through a procedure, and give the reason it wants the footage.
So I narrowed the access, and that reduced the harm to privacy. Another layer of protection. That's a great bridging recommendation against a privacy argument.
Now look. If these tasks were real situations, and you really chose the camera side, you'd really want that mechanism. Because you understand there's a real harm to privacy.
A bridging recommendation isn't there just to please the other side. Like, let's throw them a bone. No.
I really understand there are disadvantages in my position, and I want to deal with them. I want to do things properly.
Here's the full paragraph. The counter-argument, with 'on the other hand', and its explanation.
The reservation, 'at first glance... however', and our weakening: the harm is proportionate. And then its explanation.

And now, because I understand there really is a risk to privacy, I add: 'Nevertheless, since there is a genuine risk to privacy...' A body that supervises and protects. It reduces the harm to privacy.
One last small thing in that paragraph. A language slip that's easy to make.
Here's the slip: 'the danger of a break-in or leak from the database'.
Why is it wrong? Both nouns refer to the database. But a break-in is into, or to, the database. And a leak is from it.
When two words share one object, they can only share it if they take the same preposition.
The fix: give each one its own preposition. 'A break-in to the database, or a leak from it.' And 'it'... whose leak? The database's. That's obvious.
But wait. Let me stop you here.
If I chose 'yes to cameras', argued it in two paragraphs, weakened the counter-argument, and in the end I do move a little toward the other side... why wait with that until the rebuttal paragraph?
What we have here is a complex position. A plain position takes a side. Extreme right, or extreme left.
A complex position says: I choose a side, but with some reservations for edge cases or certain situations. To build in safeguards, because I understand the extreme position has disadvantages.
So why leave it for the end? You can present the complex position already in the opening paragraph. If you can keep its boundary coherent.
I took that small recommendation from the end of the rebuttal paragraph, and put it in the opening. And all through the essay, you can refer back to those safeguards.
One warning about complex positions and bridging recommendations.
'Both sides have a point' is not an answer to the question.
And if you say you support a complete ban, and then quietly allow exceptions, you've changed the proposal without saying so.
You can reject the complete version and defend a narrower one. But say so clearly. And say exactly where the line is.
And a middle position is only worth it if it answers the question, and fits your arguments.
So, to sum up. If you can keep the boundary coherent, a complex position from the opening paragraph is a good option, instead of a bridging recommendation at the end.
If you're still somewhere in the middle, and a bit worried, just add a bridging recommendation at the end of the rebuttal paragraph. Done right, it'll impress the rater too.
And either way, a bridging recommendation is optional. Finding a good one takes thought. Sometimes it's easy, sometimes it's hard. If you can't find a good one... let it go.
